disease_info: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is a trauma- and stressor-related disorder that develops after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, either directly, as a witness, or through learning about events affecting close others. It is characterized by persistent re-experiencing of the trauma, avoidance of trauma-related stimuli, negative alterations in cognitions and mood, and marked changes in arousal and reactivity lasting more than one month and causing functional impairment. The clinical course can be acute or chronic, with some individuals developing delayed onset or experiencing waxing and waning severity over years. PTSD is distinguished from other anxiety and mood disorders by the requirement of a qualifying traumatic event and the specific pattern of trauma-linked intrusions, avoidance, and hyperarousal.

narrative.personality: Cindy is a routine-loving, energetic team player with a competitive streak, who juggles structured professional responsibilities with a socially active and occasionally disorganized personal life.
narrative.stressor: About two and a half years ago, Cindy was overseeing a night-shift safety audit at the plant when a press malfunctioned and severely injured a coworker she knew well, pinning him despite multiple lockout-tagout procedures that she had personally signed off on earlier in the week. She was one of the first responders on the floor, helping to free him while witnessing extensive trauma and believing for several minutes that he might die in front of her; later investigations focused heavily on procedural lapses, and she internalized a sense of personal responsibility despite systemic factors. In the months that followed, she threw herself into extra safety trainings, overtime audits, and community workshops, while her easygoing social routines—softball league, dancing, weekend trips—became increasingly erratic as she struggled to reconcile her identity as a safety professional with the accident. Over the next two years, her functioning at work deteriorated as she avoided certain equipment and shifts, clashed with management over risk tolerance, and became so worn down by chronic exhaustion and self-doubt that she finally agreed to see a psychiatrist at the urging of her supervisor after nearly losing her job for repeated late arrivals and visible fatigue.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can't sleep through the night anymore, and it's gotten to where I'm barely functioning at work.”

narrative.personality: Albert is a pragmatic, precision-focused tinkerer whose competitive drive and skepticism of others push him to work hard and solve problems with his hands, often at the expense of his own basic needs.
narrative.stressor: Roughly two years and four months ago, Albert was driving home late from a weekend maker meetup when a speeding truck ran a red light and slammed into the side of his small car, spinning it into a light pole and trapping him inside until emergency services arrived; he watched another driver in a nearby vehicle who was critically injured and later learned that person had died. The abruptness and violence of the crash, combined with the feeling of being helplessly pinned while listening to sirens and shouting around him, left a deep impression on someone used to being in control and methodical about risk. Initially he tried to shrug it off, returning to work quickly and doubling down on his usual habits of long hours, skipped meals, and late-night projects, but he slowly became more tense and guarded in everyday situations, especially when out in public or around heavy machinery, and his friends noticed he was increasingly jumpy and on edge. When his constant scanning of intersections, exaggerated startle reactions at the shop, and mounting conflict with coworkers over “carelessness” began to jeopardize his standing at work and made it hard for him to relax even during hobbies like hiking or basketball, he finally sought psychiatric help at the suggestion of his foreman, who was concerned about his escalating tension and inability to “turn off” his alertness.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I'm constantly on guard and tense, like I can't ever relax or stop watching for something bad to happen.”

narrative.personality: Joseph is a meticulous, community-oriented retiree who enjoys structured routines, hands-on projects, and sharing local history, while tending to worry over small details.
narrative.stressor: Just over two years ago, Joseph was driving his teenage grandson home from a fishing trip when another vehicle lost control on an icy Minnesota back road and struck them head-on, causing their car to roll into a ditch; Joseph was conscious throughout, trapped in the driver’s seat, unable to reach his grandson, who died before paramedics arrived. The combination of profound grief, the shock of suddenly losing a beloved family member in such a violent and unexpected way, and his belief that he should have foreseen the danger or not driven in those conditions deeply unsettled his previously stable, detail-focused world. In the months after the accident he tried to maintain his volunteer roles at the senior center and church, but his usual pleasure in gardening, woodworking, and community events was overshadowed by a persistent sense of threat and a need to constantly check his surroundings and the well-being of others, even in familiar settings like bingo nights or the library. As his preoccupation with safety and his jumpiness in crowds began to interfere with his ability to coordinate volunteers and even sit through church services, his pastor and daughter encouraged him to see a psychiatrist to address the lingering aftereffects of the crash and his ongoing difficulty feeling at ease anywhere.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Ever since the accident, I feel on edge all the time, like I'm always bracing for something terrible to happen.”
